newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Europe's Schengen pact spreads wings.
newsitem.headline: Europe's Schengen pact spreads wings.

text.p: The Schengen agreement -- Europe's most ambitious border-free pact yet -- spread its wings on Thursday to cover the five countries of the Nordic Passport Union.

At a ceremony in Luxembourg -- which currently holds the Schengen presidency -- the 10-nation group signed accession pacts with EU members Denmark, Finland and Sweden and cooperation pacts with non-EU members Iceland and Norway.

"It's a determining moment in the history of Schengen," Luxembourg's Justice Minister Marc Fischbach said. "The Schengen space will now stretch as far as the eastern frontier of Finland to the Atlantic and the Mediterranean."

He admitted that the signing would not have an immediate impact for travellers from other Schengen countries -- Austria, France, Germany, Portugal, Spain, Luxembourg, Belgium, the Netherlands, Italy and Greece.
The new countries might not actually apply the deal until 1999 or 2000, he said, as ways would have to be found to integrate them into the already overloaded Schengen Information System computer.

It was agreed on Thursday, he said, to study how a second computer could be established. The computer system is seen as essential to preventing the free-movement zone becoming a playground for organised crime.

Norwegian Secretary of State for Justice and Police, Oeystein Maeland, whose country voted against joining the European Union, said it was cooperating with Schengen to preserve the 40-year-old Passport Union.
Oslo also wanted to play a full part in the fight against organised crime, he said.
